title: Paul's Change of Plans and the Forgiven Offender
english: … God. To plan a visit for God's sake is no mark of fickleness. When I planned to come to you, I made you that promise, not out of rashness or lightness; for when I make plans, I do not make them according to the flesh: I plan spiritual things. And one who plans spiritual things must never prove false, so that with him yes is yes and no is no.

On 2 Corinthians 1:18: Whether I come or not does not rest with me; making the plan does. If the preaching had a yes and a no, my plan to come to you would rightly have had a yes and a no as well. But if the word is true, then the plan is true through and through. I trust God that nothing we have preached is false.
On 2 Corinthians 1:19: For the Son of God, our Lord Jesus, did not prove a liar either.

On 2 Corinthians 1:20–22: Through Christ we send up the Amen to God the Father, and through God we received our confirmation in Christ. By “who sealed us” he made plain that we belong to God and are estranged from the evil one; shepherds, too, set a seal on their flocks to tell their own sheep from other people's. By saying “pledge” he indicated that we have received a small security out of knowledge, while the full gift is still owed to us; for a pledge is a part of the whole.

On 2 Corinthians 1:23–24: Since the charges against them were many, he did not want to go there and condemn them. The sentence is elliptical. He means: I did want to come to you, but not as one who is lord and teacher of your faith. Stumbling is your affair; setting right those who stumble is ours, so that we may become fellow workers in the joy that is according to God.

The second catena form adds: By joy he means the joy that is according to God, for the apostle would not have worked with them toward a worldly joy. When he says “by faith,” he hints that they fall short in works. So, since their faith is still fruitless and incomplete, he says that he is their fellow worker.
On 2 Corinthians 2:1: This is why I did not come: not to keep from grieving you, but to keep from grieving myself, and so as not to condemn some for what they are doing.

On 2 Corinthians 2:2: You grieve me and I grieve you, but not for the same reasons. You grieve me by your sins; I grieve you by my rebukes. Yet the one who feels grief makes me glad, for his grief seems to show that he has understood; whoever feels no grief plainly did not care when he was accused. So even if I grieve you, I am doing the right thing, and it leads to my own gladness at your benefit.

On 2 Corinthians 2:3: “I wrote this,” that is, that I stayed away to spare you, at the end of this letter, where it says, “lest perhaps when I come God may humble me” (2 Corinthians 12:21). I wrote for this reason: to find you, to my pleasure, already set right, so that you would not be grieved. I said this with an eye to your good, not to mine; for I know that if you see me rejoicing, you rejoice, and if you see me in pain, you are in pain. I wrote these things so that, if you want me to come, you may correct your faults before I arrive.

On 2 Corinthians 2:4: Having shown that he makes their faults his own, he revealed by his mourning and his tears the love he has for them. When he says “I wrote to you,” he means: not that you should simply be grieved, but that joy according to God should take the place of your grief.

On 2 Corinthians 2:5: If anyone has grieved me, a man who loves, he has grieved not me alone but, in part, you as well. He stops there so as not to press too hard by adding “and Christ.” He kept back the words “and Christ,” so that saying them would not weigh too heavily.
On 2 Corinthians 2:6: By “punishment” he means the condemnation passed by the majority.
On 2 Corinthians 2:7: To forgive him this.
On 2 Corinthians 2:8–9: You obeyed me when I said to condemn him; obey me also when I say to call the condemned man back.

On 2 Corinthians 2:10: “Forgive him this,” he says, “for you know that whatever you forgive this man, I too want to forgive.” In this way he shows that his affection for them makes him want to be of one mind with them.

On 2 Corinthians 2:12–13: He seems to have been grieved with the people in Troas. They had not made much of Titus or kept him there until Paul himself arrived, but, slack about the faith, they let him go. So, to bring them to their senses as unworthy, he passed them by, even though a door had been opened and no one was shutting out the preaching. Or he passed them by for this reason as well: he could easily set things right there on a later visit, since nothing stood in the way.

On 2 Corinthians 2:14: That is, to him who makes public the insults and hardships we suffer for Christ. Paul confesses it a greater grace that he is counted worthy to be led in triumph because of Christ. He also says this for the Corinthians' sake, for he feared that they might give way because of the …

added_allusions.reason: Quotes “lest ... when I come God humble me”.
“yes is yes and no is no” may echo the saying; it is also the wording of 2 Corinthians 1:17. Not cited in the text.

title: The Law as Ministry of Death vs the Spirit as Ministry of Life
english: … afflictions they were enduring, and fall away from salvation.

On 2 Corinthians 2:15–16: The idolaters are in a death of the mind because of the ignorance and hardness within them, and when they do not accept the preaching of the gospel they fall into a second death as well. But those whom the training of the law brought to the beginnings of the knowledge of God are, in a sense, already in life; yet if they believe in Christ, they receive the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father, from life to life. A little later he explains this passage differently: Those who achieve such things are the fragrance of Christ, and they are not just anyone, but those who serve God sincerely. Since such words would sound boastful, Paul does not say them of himself; but by what he adds, “For we are not like the many,” he pointed to himself.

On 2 Corinthians 2:17: By “peddling” the word he means either mixing it with circumcision and sabbath-keeping, or the way some people treat godliness as a way to make money. “I say that I speak out of sincerity”: and he says he has this very sincerity from God, not from any power of his own. He also gives another sense: we speak out of sincerity because we speak from God, not trifling with these matters but preaching a revelation from God.
The second catena form adds: He says this because there were also false apostles who counted the word about godliness a way to make money.

On 2 Corinthians 3:1: From here on he wants to show how far the law falls short of grace, so that no one from the circumcision would use the standing of Moses and the prophets to shame those from the Gentiles into keeping the law.

On 2 Corinthians 3:2–3: That is, this faith and life of yours becomes a letter to everyone and a token by which our preaching is known. “Written with the Spirit,” he says, meaning by the working of the Holy Spirit. By saying “tablets of stone” and “hearts of flesh,” he shows how far grace surpasses the law: as far as a heart is better than a lifeless tablet. He also shows how much better the grace of the Spirit is than the law, and how much higher the preaching of the apostles stands than the ministry of the prophets.
On 2 Corinthians 3:5: “From ourselves” stands for “from one another.”

On 2 Corinthians 3:6: He calls the law “letter” and grace “spirit.” The law gives commands but no help, and so it weighs down those who could not fulfill it and kills them by its punishment. The Spirit cleanses from sin and supplies the gifts, and so it plainly leads to life.

On 2 Corinthians 3:7–9: And yet the glory was not on the tablets but on Moses' face, as he says next: “because of the glory of his face, which was being done away.” Not wanting to speak against the prophet Moses, he calls Moses “the law” and aims his words at it, showing that the grace given to Moses is less than the grace of the apostles. “But if the ministry of death”: he calls Moses a ministry of death, and calls the law death, because the law, once disobeyed, brought death about. Yet this does not discredit the law, for the apostles too are called “the fragrance of death to death” (2 Corinthians 2:16). He calls the apostles a ministry of the Spirit and Moses a ministry of death. But to spare Moses he speaks of tablets: Moses brought tablets down from the mountain, while the apostles, sent into the world, brought the Spirit.

The second catena form adds: He called the apostles a fragrance of death because of those who do not obey the preaching. The fragrance of death is the threat of Gehenna, which brings eternal death on unbelievers; the fragrance of life is the preaching of the kingdom, which sends those who follow the teaching on to eternal life. A fragrance runs ahead of the thing itself. He calls Moses a minister of condemnation and of death, for in the law he condemned those who did not obey.
On 2 Corinthians 3:10: When the glorified letter of the law is weighed against the surpassing glory of the Spirit, it has not been glorified. No one would say it has been glorified in this matter …

added_allusions.reason: Quotes “a fragrance of death to death” in the note on 3:7-9.

title: Transformation from Law to Spirit
english: … of the comparison with what surpasses it.
On 2 Corinthians 3:11: He showed that the law must cease and lie idle, while the grace of the Spirit, brought in to replace it, must remain.

On 2 Corinthians 3:12–14: “Since, then, we have such a hope.” Hope that is seen is not hope (Romans 8:24). He made clear that grace remains and receives its increase even after the resurrection. “So that the children of Israel could not gaze at the end of what was being done away”: just as it was not possible to look steadily at the glory […], so they could not look at the end of the law either, that is, at the fact that the law will cease. At once he says, “To this day they have a veil.” The end of the law, once the veil is lifted and they behold the glory of the Spirit, is this: it is done away in Christ, that is, through faith in him.

The second catena form adds: Because of the blessed hope that the grace of the Spirit stays with us, we teach boldly, and we do not copy Moses' measures. By the veil over his face he signified that the Jews could not gaze and perceive that the law would come to an end and lie idle. The veil remains and does not show even a glimpse that, now that Christ has come, the law is done away.

On 2 Corinthians 3:15–16: Moses wore the veil while he spoke to the Jews but took it off when he turned back to the Lord. In the same way the Jews now, after reading the law and handing back the book, carry the veil away, as if Moses had turned back to the Lord. So if you leave and come to the Spirit, your veil is taken off, just as Moses' was when he turned back to the Lord.

On 2 Corinthians 3:17: Whoever has been counted worthy of the Spirit of the Lord has been set free from the law's condemnation, for the gifts are worked through the Spirit. And the gift is for those who are worthy.

On 2 Corinthians 3:18: “We,” he says, meaning the apostles, are seen by people with unveiled face; but when he says “we all,” he shows that the Spirit's kindness is shared by all. The Israelites could not approach the glory of Moses, but for us the glory of God is easy to approach. Once we have set ourselves firmly in faith and cleansed ourselves, we behold the glory of God as in a mirror: we see it, and in our souls, as in a mirror, we take the imprint of the image of the Spirit's glory. From knowledge under the law we are transformed into spiritual grace. Or it may be understood this way: from the glory of the Spirit at work in us we come, plainly, into the glory of adoption. “Just as” here means “inasmuch as it comes from the Lord, the Spirit.” Notice that he called the Holy Spirit Lord, not the Son of God. One person looks into a mirror, and another takes on the image of the one looking; so it is with the Spirit. Those who behold the glory of Christ as in a mirror carry away from that glory some likeness into glory; that is, they draw to themselves the glory of the spiritual image and receive it.
The second catena form adds: The glory we come from is not the law's but the Spirit's; for once we have received the washing, we come into adoption.
On 2 Corinthians 4:1: He means the ministry of grace, not that of the law; for because grace so far exceeds them, we trample our afflictions underfoot.

On 2 Corinthians 4:2: “The hidden things of shame” are the base and shameful deeds that their doers work hard to hide because they are ashamed. Base deeds have no part in openness; they slip by unnoticed in the dark.
On 2 Corinthians 4:3: Even if the gospel is veiled, it is veiled to unbelievers. It is not as it was under the law, when the glory of Moses' face was veiled from all Israel.

On 2 Corinthians 4:4: If “the god of this age” is read as one phrase, “blinded” follows in its natural order. But if the reading is “God blinded,” with the words transposed, it is like “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see” (Romans 11:8) and “I hardened Pharaoh's heart,” in the sense already explained. Just as he is called “ruler of this age” not because he is a ruler by nature, but because those he deceived made him their ruler by obeying him, so he is also called “the god of this age.” He is not truly God; he is called god from what the nations say and believe, just as the belly is called the god of gluttons (Philippians 3:19).

Quotes “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see”.
“the belly is called the god of gluttons” echoes “whose god is their belly”.
